questions.stemHtml: Mechanism of action of toxin produced by the bacterium shown in the figure:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) ADP-ribosylation of Elongation factor

 

The image shows Corynebacterium diphtheriae, a Gram-positive bacillus with characteristic angulated arrangements (Chinese letter or cuneiform appearance) and metachromatic granules. This bacterium produces diphtheria toxin, which inhibits protein synthesis by targeting elongation factor 2 (EF-2).

 

Mechanism of Action:

 

  1. Toxin Production:
    • The diphtheria toxin is an exotoxin encoded by a bacteriophage.
  2. ADP-ribosylation of EF-2:
    • The toxin catalyzes the ADP-ribosylation of EF-2, a critical factor in the elongation step of protein synthesis.
    • This modification inactivates EF-2, preventing ribosomal translocation and effectively halting protein synthesis.
  3. Result:
    • The affected cell undergoes apoptosis due to inhibited protein synthesis.
    • This action underlies the formation of the pseudomembrane in the throat of affected patients.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Increase in cAMP: 

 

This mechanism is associated with toxins like:

 

  • Cholera toxin (Vibrio cholerae)
  • Heat-labile toxin of E. coli (ETEC)
  • Pertussis toxin (Bordetella pertussis)

 

Diphtheria toxin does not act via this pathway.

 

Option B. Increase in cGMP: This mechanism is linked to the heat-stable toxin of E. coli (ETEC). Diphtheria toxin does not utilize this mechanism.

 

Option D. ADP-ribosylation of Gs protein: This is the mechanism of action of cholera toxin and pertussis toxin, which act on the Gs protein to modulate adenyl cyclase activity. Diphtheria toxin specifically targets EF-2, not Gs proteins.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The toxin of Corynebacterium diphtheriae acts by ADP-ribosylating Elongation Factor 2 (EF-2), leading to the inhibition of protein synthesis and subsequent cell death.

questions.stem: Sereny test is employed for laboratory diagnosis of:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Enteroinvasive E. Coli

 

The Sereny test is a laboratory test used to identify invasive bacterial strains, specifically Enteroinvasive E. coli (EIEC). EIEC shares similar pathogenic mechanisms with Shigella species, as both invade intestinal epithelial cells, leading to cellular destruction, diarrhea, and dysentery.

 

Mechanism of EIEC Pathogenesis:

 

1. Invasion of Enterocytes:

 

  • EIEC invades the intestinal epithelial cells and multiplies intracellularly.
  • This invasion disrupts the epithelial lining, leading to inflammation, diarrhea, and dysentery (diarrhea with blood).

 

2. Sereny Test Procedure:

 

  • A saline suspension of the suspected stool sample is prepared.
  • A few drops of the suspension are instilled into the conjunctival sac of a guinea pig’s eye.

 

 

  • If the sample contains invasive organisms like EIEC, they invade the conjunctival cells, causing conjunctivitis and keratitis within 24 hours.

 

3. Interpretation:

 

  • Positive test: Conjunctivitis and keratitis, confirming the presence of invasive strains like EIEC.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Enterotoxigenic E. coli (ETEC): ETEC produces heat-labile and heat-stable enterotoxins that act by increasing cAMP and cGMP, respectively. It does not invade the intestinal cells and cannot be detected by the Sereny test.

 

Option B. Enteropathogenic E. coli (EPEC): EPEC causes diarrhea by attaching to the intestinal epithelium and causing effacement of microvilli, disrupting absorption. It does not invade the cells and cannot be detected by the Sereny test.

 

Option C. Enterohaemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC): EHEC produces shiga-like toxins, leading to bloody diarrhea and complications such as hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS). It does not invade the intestinal cells, so the Sereny test is not applicable.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The Sereny test is specific for detecting Enteroinvasive E. coli (EIEC) by demonstrating its ability to invade epithelial cells. A positive Sereny test indicates an invasive strain causing dysentery due to intestinal cell destruction.

questions.stem: Haemophilus parainfluenzae requires which factors:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Only factor V

 

Haemophilus species require specific growth factors for cultivation:

 

  1. Factor V (NAD): A coenzyme required by certain Haemophilus species for growth.
  2. Factor X (Hemin): A growth factor derived from hemoglobin that some Haemophilus species also require.

 

Haemophilus parainfluenzae:

 

  • Requires only Factor V for growth and not Factor X.
  • It will not grow on nutrient agar unless Factor V is provided (e.g., through chocolate agar or specific supplements).

 

Summary of Factor Requirements for Haemophilus Species:

 

  • H. influenzae, H. aegypticus, and H. haemolyticus:
    • Require both Factor X and Factor V.
  • H. ducreyi:
    • Requires only Factor X.
  • Haemophilus para species (e.g., H. parainfluenzae, H. parahemolyticus, H. paraphrophilus):
    • Require only Factor V.

 

Mnemonic:

 

  1. D for Ducreyi → D for 10 (Factor X): H. ducreyi requires only Factor X.
  2. Para starts with P → P for 5 (Factor V): All Haemophilus "para" species require only Factor V.
  3. HAI (H. influenzae, H. aegypticus, H. haemolyticus) → Both Factors X and V: These species require both growth factors.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Haemophilus parainfluenzae requires only Factor V (NAD) for growth. Distinguish its growth requirement from other Haemophilus species using the mnemonic provided.

questions.stemHtml: The colonies grown in MacConkey agar belongs to:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Klebsiella

 

MacConkey agar is a differential medium used to distinguish between lactose fermenters and non-lactose fermenters among gram-negative bacteria:

 

1. Lactose Fermenters: Produce pink colonies due to acid production from lactose fermentation.

 

 

 

2. Non-Lactose Fermenters: Produce pale or yellow colonies as they do not ferment lactose.

 

 

3. Late Lactose Fermenters: Initially produce pale colonies that later turn pink.

 

 

Key Characteristics of Klebsiella on MacConkey Agar:

 

  • Pink mucoid colonies: Klebsiella is a strong lactose fermenter and produces distinct sticky, mucoid colonies due to its capsule.
  • The presence of the capsule contributes to the colony’s sticky texture and mucoid appearance.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. E. coli: E. coli also produces pink colonies on MacConkey agar as it is a lactose fermenter. However, E. coli colonies are not mucoid and lack the stickiness seen in Klebsiella colonies. The colonies of E.coli are typically flat as opposed to mucoid colonies by klebsiella.

 

 

Option B. Pseudomonas: Pseudomonas species are non-lactose fermenters and produce pale or yellow colonies on MacConkey agar. This eliminates Pseudomonas as a potential answer in this case.

 

Option D. Proteus: Proteus species are also non-lactose fermenters and produce pale colonies. Proteus colonies often exhibit swarming motility, which is absent in Klebsiella.

 

Educational Objective:

 

On MacConkey agar, Klebsiella produces pink mucoid colonies due to lactose fermentation and its capsule. This distinguishes it from other lactose fermenters like E. coli, which produce pink but non-mucoid colonies.

questions.stem: Dienes’ phenomena is seen with:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Proteus mirabilis

 

Dienes’ phenomenon is a laboratory observation used to differentiate between strains of Proteus species, particularly Proteus mirabilis. It relies on the characteristic swarming motility of Proteus bacteria.

 

Key Features:

 

1. Swarming Motility: Proteus species are highly motile and exhibit swarming on agar plates. This appears as concentric circular waves spreading outward from the inoculation site.

 

2. Dienes’ Phenomenon: 

 

  • When two strains of Proteus are inoculated on the same agar plate, their swarming patterns are observed

 

 

  • If the swarming patterns merge seamlessly: The strains are identical.
  • If a line of demarcation forms between the swarming zones: The strains are different.

 

3. Application: This phenomenon helps in identifying and distinguishing between strains of Proteus mirabilis in microbiological studies.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Klebsiella: Klebsiella species are non-motile and do not exhibit swarming. Hence, they do not show Dienes’ phenomenon.

 

Option C. Providentia: Providentia species are motile but do not exhibit the swarming motility or Dienes’ phenomenon seen in Proteus species.

 

Option D. Morganella: Morganella species are motile but do not produce the swarming motility required for Dienes’ phenomenon.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Dienes’ phenomenon is a unique characteristic of Proteus mirabilis, allowing differentiation of strains based on the merging or separation of swarming patterns on agar plates.

questions.stem: An elderly man presented with fever and cough. Sputum examination revealed gram-negative organisms that were grown on Buffered charcoal yeast extract agar. The organism involved is:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Legionella pneumophila


Buffered Charcoal Yeast Extract (BCYE) agar is a selective medium used specifically for the isolation of Legionella pneumophila, the causative agent of Legionnaires' disease. This disease often presents in elderly individuals with symptoms like fever, cough, and respiratory distress.

 

Culture

 

Buffered charcoal, yeast extract (BCYE) agar: Legionellae are highly fastidious and grow on complex media, such as BCYE agar after 3–5 days of incubation at 37°C in 5% CO2

 

 

Key Features of Legionella pneumophila:

 

  1. Gram-negative bacteria: Appears as faintly staining gram-negative bacilli in sputum smears.
  2. Growth Requirements: Requires cysteine and iron for growth, which are provided by BCYE agar.
  3. Selective Medium: BCYE agar inhibits the growth of other organisms and supports Legionella growth, making it a diagnostic clue.

 

Clinical Presentation:

 

  • Typically affects elderly or immunocompromised individuals.
  • Symptoms include fever, non-productive cough, and sometimes gastrointestinal or neurological manifestations.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. H. influenzae: H. influenzae is a gram-negative organism but does not grow on BCYE agar. It is usually grown on chocolate agar, requiring both Factor X (hemin) and Factor V (NAD).

 

Option C. Burkholderia cepacia: While Burkholderia cepacia is a gram-negative organism, it does not grow on BCYE agar. It is often associated with opportunistic infections in cystic fibrosis patients.

 

Option D. Brucella: Brucella is a gram-negative organism that typically grows on Brucella agar or blood-enriched media, not BCYE agar.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Legionella pneumophila grows on Buffered Charcoal Yeast Extract (BCYE) agar, which provides specific growth factors like cysteine and iron. The most specific diagnostic clue in this case is the use of BCYE agar for isolation.

questions.stem: A patient with history of consumption of unpasteurized milk presents with fever. Blood culture reveals gram positive organism with tumbling motility. Most probable disease:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Listeriosis

 

Listeria monocytogenes is a gram-positive bacterium that can cause listeriosis, a zoonotic disease often linked to the consumption of contaminated unpasteurized milk or dairy products.

 

Key Features of Listeria monocytogenes:

 

  1. Tumbling Motility:
    • Listeria exhibits tumbling motility at 25°C due to its peritrichous flagella (flagella distributed all around).
    • This motility is diagnostic and differentiates it from other organisms.
  2. Source of Infection:
    • Listeriosis is associated with contaminated food products such as unpasteurized milk, soft cheeses, and deli meats.
    • It is a zoonotic disease transmitted from animals to humans.
  3. Clinical Manifestations:
    • Fever, diarrhea, and flu-like symptoms in healthy individuals.
    • Severe forms: Can lead to meningitis, encephalitis, or septicemia in immunocompromised individuals, the elderly, pregnant women, and neonates.
  4. Differential Motility:
    • Motile at 25°C but non-motile at 37°C.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Bovine tuberculosis: Caused by Mycobacterium bovis, a gram-positive, acid-fast organism. It does not exhibit tumbling motility and is primarily diagnosed with Ziehl-Neelsen staining.

 

Option C. Brucella: Brucella species are gram-negative bacteria that cause brucellosis. They are associated with unpasteurized milk but do not show tumbling motility.

 

Option D. Anthrax: Caused by Bacillus anthracis, a gram-positive organism, but it does not exhibit tumbling motility. Anthrax is more commonly associated with skin ulcers and inhalational symptoms rather than fever after milk consumption.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Listeria monocytogenes is the only organism among the options that exhibits tumbling motility and is associated with consumption of unpasteurized milk, making it the most probable cause in this case.

questions.stem: In reference to the Mycoplasma, the following are true except:

options.label: B
options.text: They can reproduce in cell free media

options.label: C
options.text: They have an affinity for mammalian cell membranes

options.label: D
options.text: They can pass through filters of 450 nm pore size

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) They are inhibited by penicillin

 

Mycoplasma are unique bacteria distinguished by their lack of a cell wall. This absence of a cell wall has significant implications for their biology and susceptibility to antibiotics.

 

They are inhibited by penicillin is false. Penicillin and other beta-lactam antibiotics target bacterial cell wall synthesis. Since Mycoplasma lack a cell wall, they are inherently resistant to these drugs

 

Key Features of Mycoplasma:

 

  1. Lack of Cell Wall: Mycoplasma species are the only bacteria that naturally lack a cell wall. This allows them to be pleomorphic (variable in shape) and resistant to antibiotics targeting cell wall synthesis, such as penicillins and other beta-lactam antibiotics.
  2. Reproduction in Cell-Free Media: Mycoplasma can reproduce in artificial cell-free media, such as broth or agar supplemented with specific nutrients, including sterols required for membrane synthesis. Colonies of Mycoplasma have a characteristic "fried egg" appearance.
  3. Affinity for Mammalian Cell Membranes: Mycoplasma have a strong affinity for mammalian cell membranes due to their incorporation of sterols from the host, enhancing their membrane stability and interaction with host cells.
  4. Filterability: Mycoplasma can pass through filters with pore sizes of 450 nm due to their small size and flexibility, unlike most other bacteria.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Mycoplasma lack a cell wall, making them resistant to penicillin and other beta-lactam antibiotics. Their unique features include the ability to pass through filters, reproduce in cell-free media, and exhibit affinity for mammalian cell membranes.

questions.stem: Selective medium for meningococcal infection is:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Thayer Martin medium

 

The Thayer-Martin medium is a selective medium specifically designed for the growth of Neisseria species, including:

 

  • Neisseria meningitidis (causative agent of meningococcal infection)
  • Neisseria gonorrhoeae

 

Composition of Thayer-Martin Medium:

 

  1. Vancomycin: Inhibits gram-positive bacteria.
  2. Colistin: Inhibits gram-negative bacteria (excluding Neisseria).
  3. Nystatin: Inhibits fungal growth.

 

These antibiotics make Thayer-Martin medium selective for Neisseria species by suppressing the growth of other organisms.

 

Differentiating Neisseria meningitidis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae:

 

Toxic shock syndrome 

 

 

Culture on Other Media:

 

  • Both grow on blood agar and chocolate agar but require Thayer-Martin medium for selective isolation.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. DCA (Deoxycholate Citrate Agar): Selective for gram-negative enteric bacteria like Salmonella and Shigella. Not suitable for Neisseria species.

 

Option B. Blood agar: Non-selective medium that supports the growth of a variety of organisms, including Neisseria, but does not prevent the growth of other bacteria.

 

Option C. LJ medium (Lowenstein-Jensen medium): Used for Mycobacterium species (e.g., M. tuberculosis). Irrelevant for Neisseria.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Thayer-Martin medium is the selective medium of choice for isolating Neisseria meningitidis, as it selectively supports Neisseria growth by inhibiting other bacteria and fungi through its antibiotic composition.

questions.stem: Differentiating feature of Neisseria gonococcus from Neisseria meningitidis is:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Maltose fermentation

 

The primary differentiating feature between Neisseria gonorrhoeae (gonococcus) and Neisseria meningitidis (meningococcus) is their ability to ferment specific sugars:

 

  1. Glucose Fermentation:
    • Both N. gonorrhoeae and N. meningitidis ferment glucose.
  2. Maltose Fermentation:
    • N. meningitidis ferments maltose.
    • N. gonorrhoeae does not ferment maltose.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Options A. Lactose Fermentation, C. Mannitol Fermentation and D. Sucrose Fermentation: Neither species ferments lactose, mannitol, or sucrose.

 

Summary of Key Differences:

 

  • Capsulation:
    • N. meningitidis: Encapsulated (capsule is the main virulence factor).
    • N. gonorrhoeae: Non-encapsulated (pili serve as the main virulence factor).
  • Clinical Manifestation:
    • N. meningitidis: Causes meningitis and septicemia.
    • N. gonorrhoeae: Causes gonorrhea, pelvic inflammatory disease, and other localized infections.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The differentiating feature between N. gonorrhoeae and N. meningitidis is maltose fermentation. N. meningitidis ferments maltose, while N. gonorrhoeae does not.

questions.stem: Pseudomonas exhibits protein synthesis by inhibiting:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) EF-2

 

Pseudomonas aeruginosa produces Exotoxin A, which inhibits protein synthesis by targeting elongation factor 2 (EF-2). This mechanism disrupts ribosomal translocation, effectively halting protein synthesis and leading to cell death.

 

Mechanism of Action:

 

  1. Exotoxin A:
    • ADP-ribosylates EF-2, rendering it nonfunctional.
    • EF-2 is essential for translocation during protein synthesis on the ribosome.
  2. Effect on Host Cells:
    • The inhibition of EF-2 halts protein synthesis, resulting in cell death.

 

DPSS Mnemonic:

 

The four bacteria that inhibit protein synthesis by targeting EF-2 are:

 

  • D: Corynebacterium diphtheriae (Diphtheria toxin)
  • P: Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Exotoxin A)
  • S: Shigella dysenteriae (Shiga toxin)
  • S: Shiga-like toxin (produced by Enterohemorrhagic E. coli, EHEC)

 

Note:

 

Toxins that act by increasing cAMP

 

BVEB

 

  • Bacillus anthrax
  • Vibrio
  • ETEC
  • Bordetella

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. RNA polymerase: Inhibition of RNA polymerase is the mechanism of action for rifampin or toxins like the alpha-amanitin from mushrooms but is not relevant to Pseudomonas.

 

Option C. Transpeptidase: This enzyme is targeted by beta-lactam antibiotics, not by Pseudomonas exotoxins.

 

Option D. Reverse transcriptase: Reverse transcriptase is an enzyme found in retroviruses like HIV and is not involved in Pseudomonas infection.

 

Educational Objective: 

 

Pseudomonas aeruginosa inhibits protein synthesis through Exotoxin A, which ADP-ribosylates EF-2, making it a critical virulence factor.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old boy went for trekking, came with a history of rash. Weil Felix test revealed elevated Ox 2 and Ox 19 titres. What is the most likely organism?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Rickettsia rickettsiae

 

The Weil-Felix test is a serological test used to diagnose Rickettsial infections by detecting cross-reacting antibodies against Proteus antigens (OX2, OX19, and OXK).

 

Key Points:

 

  • Rickettsia rickettsii (Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever):
    • Causes spotted fever group disease.
    • Both OX19 and OX2 titres are elevated in the Weil-Felix test.
    • Transmitted by ticks.
  • Differentiation of Rickettsial Infections:
    • Typhus Group:
      • Includes R. prowazekii (epidemic typhus) and R. typhi (endemic typhus).
      • Only OX19 is elevated.
    • Spotted Fever Group:
      • Includes R. rickettsii (Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever), R. conorii (Indian Tick Typhus).
      • Both OX19 and OX2 are elevated.
    • Rickettsial Pox:
      • Caused by R. akari.
      • No elevation of OX antigens.

 

Summary of Key Rickettsial Groups:

 

 

Educational Objective:

 

The presence of elevated OX19 and OX2 titres in a Weil-Felix test strongly indicates a tick-borne spotted fever group infection, most likely caused by Rickettsia rickettsii (Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever).

questions.stem: In a patient with typhoid, diagnosis after 12 days of onset of fever is best done by:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Widal

 

Typhoid fever, caused by the bacteria Salmonella typhi, progresses through distinct phases where the diagnostic method depends on the stage of the disease:

 

  1. Week 1: Blood culture is the most reliable method as the bacteria is present in the bloodstream during the early phase.
  2. Week 2: Antibody detection becomes important. This is done through the Widal test, which detects antibodies against the O and H antigens of Salmonella typhi in the patient’s blood.
  3. Week 3: Stool culture is used as the bacteria is excreted in the feces during this phase.
  4. Week 4: Urine culture becomes relevant as the bacteria can be excreted in the urine.

 

Since the question specifies 12 days after onset of fever, this falls within the second week of the disease. Therefore, the appropriate diagnostic test is the Widal test, which detects antibodies in the blood.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The Widal test is the diagnostic method of choice in the second week (7–14 days) of typhoid fever as it detects antibodies against Salmonella typhi.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old female presented to the hospital on the third day of menstruation with complaints of high fever, vomiting and a rash on her trunk and extremities. On investigation she had leucocytosis and a negative blood culture. She is diagnosed as:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Toxic shock syndrome

 

Toxic shock syndrome (TSS) is a life-threatening condition caused by bacterial toxins, most commonly the toxic shock syndrome toxin (TSST-1) produced by Staphylococcus aureus. This condition is frequently associated with menstruating women who use high-absorbency tampons, which can facilitate the growth of S. aureus and release of toxins.

 

Key Features of the Case:

 

  1. Menstrual Association: The patient presented on the third day of menstruation.
  2. Clinical Symptoms: High fever, vomiting, and rash on the trunk and extremities are hallmark features of TSS.
  3. Investigations: Leucocytosis and negative blood culture further support the diagnosis, as TSS is toxin-mediated and does not always involve bacteremia.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Staphylococcal food poisoning:

 

  • Typically presents with acute gastroenteritis (nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramps) within hours of consuming contaminated food. Rash and menstrual association are not seen.
  • Occurs after eating meat and fish, or milk and milk products as custards or potato salad.
  • Site of action: The toxin stimulates the vagus nerve and vomiting center of the brain. It also stimulates the intestinal peristaltic activity

 

Option B. Scalded skin syndrome:

 

  • Caused by exfoliative toxins of Staphylococcus aureus. It features separation of the epidermis from the dermis (Nikolsky’s sign positive) rather than the rash described in the question.
  • Responsible for ‘staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome’ (SSSS), exfoliative skin diseases.
  • Outer layer of epidermis gets separated from the underlying tissues.

 

 

Option D. Varicella zoster infection: Presents with a vesicular rash in a "dew drop on rose petal" pattern, typically associated with systemic symptoms. It does not match the menstrual association or the symptoms described.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Toxic shock syndrome should be suspected in menstruating women presenting with high fever, vomiting, rash, and systemic signs of infection, especially with tampon use. The causative agent is Staphylococcus aureus, producing toxic shock syndrome toxin (TSST-1).

questions.stem: A child presents with infective skin lesion of the leg. Culture was done which showed Gram-positive cocci in chains which were Beta hemolytic colonies. The test to confirm the organism is:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Bacitracin sensitivity

 

The culture reveals Gram-positive cocci in chains, a characteristic feature of Streptococcus species. Additionally, the beta-hemolytic property on blood agar indicates the organism could belong to Group A or Group B streptococci. The presence of infective skin lesions further narrows the diagnosis to Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A Streptococcus), as it is the most common cause of such infections.

 

 

Key Features of the Case:

 

  1. Gram-Positive Cocci in Chains: Distinguishes Streptococcus from Staphylococcus (which occurs in clusters).
  2. Beta Hemolysis: Indicates complete hemolysis, typical of certain streptococci groups.
  3. Infective Skin Lesion: Strongly associated with Group A Streptococcus infections such as impetigo, cellulitis, or erysipelas.

 

To confirm Streptococcus pyogenes, bacitracin sensitivity testing is performed, as Group A streptococci are sensitive to bacitracin.

 

Additional information:

 

Gram positive Cocci

 

  • Staphylococcus
  • Streptococcus

 

 

 

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Bile solubility: This test is used to identify Streptococcus pneumoniae, which is alpha-hemolytic and not associated with beta-hemolytic skin infections.

 

Option B. Optochin sensitivity: Optochin sensitivity testing differentiates Streptococcus pneumoniae from other alpha-hemolytic streptococci. It is not relevant for beta-hemolytic streptococci.

 

Option D. Catalase positive: Catalase testing distinguishes Streptococcus (catalase-negative) from Staphylococcus (catalase-positive). While the result is helpful in classification, it does not confirm the specific organism in this case.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A Streptococcus) is the most common cause of infective skin lesions and can be confirmed through bacitracin sensitivity testing.

questions.stemHtml: A 9-years old child presented to OPD with complaints of high grade fever, vomiting, one episode of seizure. CSF examination was done and Gram staining of the culture showed the following finding. What is the probable causative agent?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Streptococcus pneumonia

 

The findings are consistent with Streptococcus pneumoniae (pneumococcus), a common cause of bacterial meningitis in children. The diagnosis is supported by the following:

 

  1. Clinical Presentation: The child presented with fever, vomiting, and a seizure, which are typical signs of meningitis.
  2. CSF Findings: The Gram-stained image shows Gram-positive diplococci (purple in color, cocci arranged in pairs), a hallmark of Streptococcus pneumoniae.
  3. Shape and Color: Streptococcus pneumoniae appears as flame-shaped diplococci, which are Gram-positive (violet).

 

This organism is known to cause meningitis, pneumonia, and otitis media in children, especially those under the age of 10.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Hemophilus influenzae: This organism appears as small, pleomorphic Gram-negative coccobacilli. It was historically a common cause of meningitis but is now less prevalent due to widespread vaccination with the Hib vaccine.

 

Option B. Neisseria meningitides: Appears as Gram-negative diplococci. It is another major cause of meningitis but is excluded here due to the Gram-positive nature of the organism in the image.

 

Option D. Escherichia coli: Appears as Gram-negative rods and is more commonly associated with neonatal meningitis. The organism in the image is clearly cocci and not bacilli.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The identification of Gram-positive diplococci in CSF Gram stain is diagnostic of Streptococcus pneumoniae, a major cause of bacterial meningitis in children.

questions.stem: False about mechanism of bacterial toxins:

options.label: A
options.text: Cholera toxin acts by inhibition of guanylcyclase

options.label: C
options.text: Shiga toxin act by inhibiting protein synthesis

options.label: D
options.text: Diphtheria toxin act by inhibiting protein synthesis

questions.answerText: Cholera toxin acts by inhibition of guanylcyclase
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Cholera toxin acts by inhibition of guanylcyclase

 

Cholera toxin (produced by Vibrio cholerae) does not inhibit guanyl cyclase. Instead, it stimulates adenyl cyclase, leading to increased levels of cyclic AMP (cAMP). This results in massive fluid and electrolyte loss, causing severe watery diarrhea. 

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Botulinum toxin inhibits Ach release: This is true. It is a hallmark feature of botulinum toxin action, resulting in flaccid paralysis.

 

Option C. Shiga toxin acts by inhibiting protein synthesis: This is true. Shiga toxin targets ribosomes, leading to inhibition of protein synthesis and cellular damage.

 

Option D. Diphtheria toxin acts by inhibiting protein synthesis: This is true. Diphtheria toxin inactivates EF-2, preventing protein synthesis and causing cell death.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Cholera toxin increases cAMP levels by stimulating adenyl cyclase, not by inhibiting guanyl cyclase.
  • Shiga and diphtheria toxins inhibit protein synthesis, while botulinum toxin blocks acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction.
